Title: A Practical Approach to Defining a Framework for Developing an Agentic AIOps System
Authors: Răzvan Daniel Zota; Corneliu Bărbulescu; Radu Constantinescu
Core Problem Addressed: Conventional AIOps systems are limited to observability and predefined rules with reactive responses, lacking autonomy to proactively detect and resolve incidents without human input; critical tasks such as incident resolution and problem management still require significant human intervention, and there is no canonical definition of Agentic AIOps (Sec. 1, pp. 1-3).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A three-dimensional development framework for an Agentic AIOps system: (1) process model dimension aligned with ITIL via IBM's UPF-IT/PRM-IT (Event Management, Service Execution, Request Fulfillment, Incident Management, Problem Management); (2) service element dimension (applications, platform/middleware, infrastructure); (3) capability dimension following the Understand-Decide-Take Action paradigm; an Orchestrator component controls flow across components: discriminative AI for incident classification, RAG for diagnosis, automation components (e.g., Jenkins pipeline, Ansible playbook) for resolution, and an AI-LLM component for closure communication; autonomy is deployed progressively across ten levels with human oversight at critical decision points (Sec. 4.1-4.3, pp. 11-16; Sec. 3.1, p. 9).
Methodology: Conceptual framework proposal (vision paper) grounded in: a systematic literature review of academic articles, industry reports and white papers from the last five years (140+ articles filtered to 42 high-impact studies); the authors' own IT industry experience (IBM UPF-IT, Watson AIOps, Splunk); and focus group discussions plus semi-structured interviews with IT professionals, AI researchers, and AIOps practitioners; no prototype, deployment, or experimental evaluation (Sec. 2.1-2.4, pp. 4-5).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified quantitatively — no baselines or measured values reported; qualitative claims only: the authors state such a system "can significantly reduce incident response time" and enable self-healing IT environments, and Table 2 lists "Reduce Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR)" as the end goal of AIOps (Abstract, p. 1; Table 2, p. 7).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: No empirical efficacy results; the framework contributes design principles for reliable autonomy: progressive autonomy over ten defined levels matched to risk tolerance, process standardization via ITIL/UPF-IT, service-aware design across layers, continuous learning feedback loops, and human oversight for high-risk actions; an orchestrator manages end-to-end control flow across specialized AI/automation components; the paper also proposes a definition of Agentic AIOps as agents operating at different levels of autonomy (Sec. 4.3, pp. 14-16; Sec. 4, p. 11; Sec. 3.1, p. 9).
Limitations / Future Work: Authors acknowledge "currently we do not have experimental results that materialize the presented view" (vision of the future of Agentic AIOps) and that security concerns are out of scope; future work: defining system capabilities per ITIL Operations process, specifying components per technology (infrastructure, middleware, application), and proposing a conceptual architecture; ethical/governance considerations (accountability, transparency, oversight, KPI monitoring) are flagged as needing attention (Sec. 5, pp. 16-17).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper provides a structured conceptual foundation for positioning an Agentic AI copilot within incident response: its Understand-Decide-Take Action paradigm and the incident management mapping (classification, RAG-based diagnosis, automated resolution, LLM-based closure) mirror the pipeline a copilot would support to reduce MTTD and MTTR. The ten-level autonomy scale and progressive-autonomy principle offer a vocabulary for characterizing the copilot (human-in-the-loop) versus fully autonomous operation. Its alignment with ITIL/UPF-IT grounds the thesis in service management practice. However, it offers no empirical MTTD/MTTR evidence, so it serves as a framing and architecture reference rather than a source of quantitative benchmarks.
Relevance Score: Medium — directly proposes an agentic AIOps framework for autonomous incident detection, diagnosis, and resolution, but it is purely conceptual and reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements.

Title: Application of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity: A Systematic Literature Review
Authors: Ismayil Hasanov; Seppo Virtanen; Antti Hakkala; Jouni Isoaho
Core Problem Addressed: Clear lack of holistic systematic studies on the application and impact of LLMs in cybersecurity: existing surveys cover only single aspects (defensive, offensive, or ethical) and many are non-peer-reviewed preprints, preventing a broader understanding of this emerging technology (Sec. I, pp. 176751-176752)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Not applicable (secondary study; no system is proposed). The SLR catalogs AI/LLM uses in defensive and offensive cybersecurity, cyberethics, law, and governance; agent-style approaches surveyed include LLM agents in the NetSecGame environment, PENTESTGPT (Reasoning, Generation, and Parsing modules), Auto-GPT, Wintermute (LLM-guided privilege escalation), and the Cyber Sentinel GPT-4 dialogue system integrating an IoC signature database, SIEM, and LLM (Sec. IV-F, pp. 176767-176768; Sec. IV-G, pp. 176768-176769)
Methodology: Systematic Literature Review (simplified adaptation of the Kitchenham Guidelines and PRISMA); 8 databases/platforms (arXiv, IEEE Xplore, ResearchGate, Scopus, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, ACM Digital Library) queried with 26 keyword sets; 250 articles screened, 177 (2018-March 2024) retained and classified into 7 topical categories; 68% of the reviewed literature published in 2023 (Abstract; Sec. II, pp. 176753-176755)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — no quantified MTTD, MTTR, or alert-fatigue metrics are reported; qualitative findings only: surveyed studies note "accelerated response times due to AI's automation of the analysis and prioritization of security alerts" and that AI/ML in Open XDR enables real-time detection, reduces false positives, and enhances the overall efficiency of cybersecurity operations (Sec. IV-C3, p. 176760; Sec. IV-C5, p. 176761)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: LLM agents in NetSecGame "can surpass traditional reinforcement learning agents and human testers in planning and executing complex cybersecurity tasks," notwithstanding challenges like cost and model instability; PENTESTGPT is superior to default ChatGPT but faces challenges maintaining context; ChatGPT/Auto-GPT generate functional malicious code within minutes; in Wintermute, GPT-4 outperforms GPT-3.5-turbo and Llama2, but LLMs often repeated enumeration commands and failed to exploit found vulnerabilities effectively (Sec. IV-G, pp. 176768-176769; Sec. IV-F, pp. 176767-176768)
Limitations / Future Work: Only the abstract, introduction, discussion, and conclusion of each article were analyzed in detail (main content browsed cursorily); review cut-off March 2024; surveyed LLMs exhibit hallucinations and higher error rates without domain-specific training, requiring human oversight; the authors identify the absence of studies on LLMs for network traffic analysis / network security as a research gap and propose training an LLM to classify packet streams as legitimate or malicious (Sec. II, p. 176754; Sec. V, pp. 176771-176772; Sec. VI, pp. 176772-176773)
Relevance to My Thesis: This SLR maps the LLM-in-security landscape that an Agentic AI incident-response copilot would inhabit, consolidating evidence that LLMs are effective in log analysis, threat detection, and explainable alert triage. Its survey of agent-style systems (NetSecGame agents surpassing RL baselines and human testers, PENTESTGPT, Cyber Sentinel, HuntGPT) supports the feasibility of agentic designs for security operations. Its findings on hallucination, cost, and model instability directly motivate the human-in-the-loop copilot framing of the thesis. However, it reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements, so it serves as background and related work rather than a metric baseline.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent work: it consolidates LLM-based detection/response and LLM-agent evidence relevant to AIOps-style security operations but does not measure MTTD/MTTR with an agentic approach.

Title: Anomaly Detection and Root Cause Analysis in Cloud-Native Environments Using Large Language Models and Bayesian Networks
Authors: Diego Frazatto Pedroso; Luís Almeida; Lucas Eduardo Gulka Pulcinelli; William Akihiro Alves Aisawa; Inês Dutra; Sarita Mazzini Bruschi
Core Problem Addressed: Microservices-oriented cloud-native systems generate exponentially growing volumes of unstructured logs from many layers, making manual root cause analysis labor-intensive and prone to prolonged downtime, while constant deploys make predefined static alert thresholds ineffective; existing tools also produce complex, lengthy root-cause reports that users without deep ecosystem context cannot interpret (Sec. I, pp. 77550-77551)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: MAIA framework: Llama-3 8b fine-tuned on unstructured logs from normal execution predicts the next log message from a sequence of 10 prior logs; an anomaly is flagged when cosine similarity (MPNet sentence-similarity model) between registered and generated log blocks falls below a 0.8 threshold; detected anomalies are queued via Amazon SQS to Baynet, a dynamic Bayesian network (pgmpy) that analyzes Grafana Tempo/Istio traces, scores service health (duration, 2xx rate, P99, 5xx codes, recent-deploy TTL), and infers per-microservice outage probabilities shown in a Grafana NodeGraph; a ChatBot powered by the same LLM lets users ask questions about the detected incident — a single-LLM pipeline, not a multi-agent orchestration (Abstract; Sec. IV-V, pp. 77554-77560)
Methodology: Prototype deployment with controlled chaos-engineering experiments: Istio sock-shop e-commerce application (12 microservices; Java/JavaScript/Go; MySQL, MongoDB, RabbitMQ) on AWS EKS with Istio; ~1-hour Locust load tests generated normal-execution training logs collected via Grafana Loki to S3; Chaos Mesh injected 13 fault scenarios (pod kill, network partition, IO, memory, bandwidth, HTTP faults) in 30-minute tests (10 min baseline, 10 min faults averaging ~10 min, 10 min recovery), automated via CircleCI; ~10% of the log dataset was manually classified as ground truth; evaluation via accuracy, precision, recall, F1 heatmap per scenario (Sec. III-V, pp. 77554-77558; Sec. VI, p. 77561)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — MTTD/MTTR are not measured; the motivation states ML can help "decrease the incident time, including: find root cause, mitigation and system repair time" (Sec. I, p. 77551); detection results: precision ~1.00 in almost all tests, recall varies — Cache Disconnected Failure 1.00 on all metrics, Mongo IO Failure lowest (recall 0.71, accuracy 0.78, F1 0.83), Queue Network Disconnect recall 0.83 with 64 false negatives, most other scenarios above 0.95; the authors note false positives "remain within acceptable limits" and that unsupervised refinement is needed to "mitigate alert fatigue" (Abstract; Sec. II, p. 77554; Sec. VI, pp. 77561-77562)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Not applicable — no agentic or multi-agent architecture is evaluated; the contribution claims novelty in combining LLM insights and Bayesian networks with an interactive chat interface for user engagement, and the related work notes LLM limitations of computational cost, interpretability, and bias; the Bayesian RCA correctly ranked the injected service as root cause (front-end 90.0% outage probability; shipping 78% with dependent orders at 12.16%, showing cascading dependency effects) (Sec. II-A, p. 77552; Sec. VI-B, pp. 77562-77563)
Limitations / Future Work: False positives persist and false negatives are the primary issue (low recall on Mongo IO 0.71 and Queue Disconnect 0.83); perfect Cache Disconnected score may indicate overfitting and needs validation; the LLM neglects numerically significant log values (IPs, response times, status codes), for which LSTM networks are suggested; future work: map all error-type/microservice relationships, run systematic experiments applying each error type to all microservices, enhance model training with wider error scenarios, iterate evaluation, and optionally swap the language-modeling head for a classification head (Sec. VI, pp. 77561-77562; Sec. VII, pp. 77563)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is a strong AIOps reference for the detection and diagnosis stages that precede MTTD/MTTR reduction: it demonstrates an LLM fine-tuned on normal logs as an unsupervised anomaly detector plus a dynamic Bayesian network for probabilistic root cause localization in a Kubernetes microservices environment. Its ChatBot for querying detected incidents anticipates the copilot-style human interaction central to my research, though without agent orchestration or autonomy. The experimental protocol — sock-shop on EKS, Locust load generation, Chaos Mesh fault injection with baseline/fault/recovery windows, and manually labeled ground truth — is directly reusable for my thesis evaluation design. Its explicit mention of alert fatigue and per-scenario precision/recall reporting offers baseline metrics my agentic approach could extend toward actual MTTD/MTTR measurement.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent AIOps/observability work: LLM-based log anomaly detection with Bayesian RCA and a chat interface, but it measures detection quality (precision/recall/F1) rather than MTTD/MTTR and employs no agentic or multi-agent architecture.

Title: From LLM Reasoning to Autonomous AI Agents: A Comprehensive Review
Authors: Mohamed Amine Ferrag; Norbert Tihanyi; Mérouane Debbah
Core Problem Addressed: The landscape of evaluation benchmarks, AI-agent frameworks, and agent collaboration protocols for LLMs and autonomous AI agents is fragmented and lacks a unified taxonomy or comprehensive survey, despite a growing need for standardized evaluation and integration (Abstract, p. 84237; Sec. I, p. 84238).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Survey that consolidates the field: side-by-side comparison of benchmarks (2019–2025); taxonomy of approx. 60 LLM/AI-agent benchmarks in 8 categories; review of AI-agent frameworks (2023–2025) integrating LLMs with modular toolkits for autonomous decision-making and multi-step reasoning (LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, Swarm, OpenAI Agents SDK); applications in healthcare, materials science, software engineering, finance, etc.; agent-to-agent protocols ACP, MCP, and A2A; human-in-the-loop patterns (User Confirmation and Return of Control in Amazon Bedrock Agents) (Sec. I, p. 84238; Sec. IV, pp. 84251–84277).
Methodology: Comprehensive literature review (secondary study) with comparative tables and a taxonomy covering approx. 60 benchmarks (2019–2025), AI-agent frameworks and applications (2023–2025), 3 agent protocols, and 3 training datasets; no empirical experiment of its own and no formal SLR protocol (search strings, inclusion/exclusion criteria) is reported (Sec. I, p. 84238; Sec. III, p. 84242; Sec. IV, p. 84251).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — theoretical survey of LLM/agent benchmarks, frameworks, and protocols; incident response, MTTD, MTTR, and alert fatigue are not addressed, and reported quantitative results concern benchmark performance only (Sec. III, pp. 84242–84250).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Reports third-party results: Agent-as-a-Judge reaches 90% alignment with human judgments vs. 60–70% for LLM-as-a-Judge, cutting evaluation cost to approx. 2.29% ($30.58 vs. $1,297.50) and time to 118.43 minutes vs. 86.5 hours (Sec. III-H, p. 84246); in MultiAgentBench, cognitive planning gives a 3% improvement in milestone achievement while "adding more agents can decrease performance" (Sec. III-U, p. 84249); a study of 5 frameworks across 150 tasks identifies 14 failure modes of multi-agent LLM systems in 3 categories (design/specification shortcomings, inter-agent misalignment, task verification and termination) (Sec. V-B, p. 84278); MCP's decentralized design lacks standardized authentication and robust logging, raising security risks (Sec. V-F, p. 84279).
Limitations / Future Work: Open problems listed by the authors: advanced reasoning strategies (Meta-CoT), understanding failure modes in multi-agent LLM systems, automated scientific discovery, dynamic tool integration via reinforcement learning, integrated search via RL, and security vulnerabilities in agent protocols (Sec. V, pp. 84278–84279); remaining challenges include "automating multi-step reasoning without human oversight, balancing structured guidance with model flexibility, and integrating long-context retrieval at scale" (Sec. VI, p. 84279); no limitations of the survey method itself are stated (Not specified).
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey supplies the conceptual backbone for the agentic layer of the thesis: its taxonomy of AI-agent frameworks (LangChain, CrewAI, Swarm, Agents SDK) and of the ACP/MCP/A2A protocols directly informs architecture and orchestration choices for an Agentic AI Copilot. The catalogued multi-agent failure modes and MCP security vulnerabilities work as a ready-made risk checklist for deploying a copilot in incident response pipelines. The HITL patterns (User Confirmation, Return of Control) map onto approval gates for remediation actions that affect MTTR. Since it contains no incident-management or observability evidence, it supports the design and related-work chapters rather than the MTTD/MTTR evaluation itself.
Relevance Score: Medium — foundational survey of Agentic AI frameworks, multi-agent failure modes, protocols, and HITL patterns adjacent to the thesis architecture, but it does not address incident response or measure MTTD/MTTR.

Title: Telemetry and Agentic AI: Foundations for Optical Network Automation
Authors: Sergio Cruzes
Year & Venue: 2026; IEEE Access, vol. 14 (received 11 December 2025, accepted 24 December 2025, date of publication 30 December 2025, date of current version 20 January 2026); DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3649768
Core Problem Addressed: Optical networks carry ever-growing traffic over heterogeneous multi-vendor equipment under strict physical constraints, making traditional management hard to maintain and demanding earlier impairment detection, faster reaction, and coordinated control across domains; prior literature treats telemetry, ML, digital twins (DTs), and agentic components mostly in isolation, leaving no unified view of how they interact within closed automation loops (Sec. I, pp. 8800-8801; Sec. II, pp. 8801-8802)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Survey plus architectural synthesis: a unified framework in which telemetry acts as the sensory layer, AI/ML models provide inference and prediction, DTs stay aligned with the physical network and validate candidate actions, and agentic AI structures coordinate decisions (Sec. I, pp. 8800-8801); a reference agentic architecture synthesized from literature with four layers - event-driven data streaming (Kafka, gRPC, MQTT, Redis), a multi-agent system (MAS) layer of specialized agents (monitoring, fault analysis, QoT, RSA, DT, execution), an LLM integration layer (multimodal encoder, RAG, LoRA tuning) as reasoning core for intent parsing and plan generation, and a control/validation infrastructure that routes candidate actions through DT simulation (e.g., GNPy) and policy checks before SDN execution (Sec. VI-K, Fig. 9, p. 8818; Sec. IV-D, p. 8811); agents are built on role, perception, reasoning, memory, action, and learning capabilities, with human-in-the-loop escalation for high-impact actions (Sec. VI-G, pp. 8817-8818; Sec. VI-E, p. 8817)
Methodology: Literature survey combined with an architectural synthesis; all components are derived from prior literature and operational practice - "No new protocol, algorithm, or control mechanism is proposed" (Sec. I, p. 8801); no experiment, dataset, environment, or sample size is reported by the author; four illustrative implementation examples (soft-failure detection, spectrum reallocation, amplifier gain adjustment, network expansion) reflect patterns from already-reported implementations, complemented by a table of published demonstrations (Sec. VII-G, Table 10, pp. 8826-8829) and a synthesis of common trends (Sec. X, pp. 8832-8833)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD and MTTR are not mentioned or measured; the stated goals are qualitative - detect impairments earlier and react faster (Abstract, p. 8800); quantitative figures are cited from surveyed literature rather than measured: edge feature extraction can shrink telemetry volume "by more than 99%" while supporting sub-second processing (Sec. III-D, p. 8803); hybrid pipelines combining LLM reasoning with lightweight classifiers "reduce decision latency by 40-60 percent", distributed designs reduce end-to-end latency by factors of the order of 3-5 versus fully centralized designs, and Kafka enables delivery intervals of the order of 100 ms (Sec. III-G, p. 8805); an amplifier-gain example "reduced restoration time" with no numbers given (Sec. VII-G, p. 8826)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Contrasts rule-based automation with agentic AI on adaptability, coordination, scalability, and closed-loop suitability (Table 6, p. 8815); catalogs MAS failure modes with safeguards - conflicting agent decisions (single commit point, per-resource action locking), stale telemetry (timestamps, freshness thresholds, heartbeat topics), DT desynchronization (continuous reconciliation, authority downgrade), LLM hallucinations (restrict LLM to planning/explanation, schema validation, tool gating, human-in-the-loop), and cascading automation errors (rate limits, cool-down timers, rollback, incident-level memory) (Sec. VI-E, p. 8817); describes deployment patterns (orchestrator-worker, hierarchical, blackboard, market-oriented) (Sec. VI-H, p. 8818); discusses latency/cost optimization (quantization, speculative decoding, continuous batching, token-based API cost growth) (Sec. VI-J, p. 8818; Sec. VIII-E, p. 8829); maps telemetry and agentic AI onto TM Forum autonomy levels L0-L5 (Sec. VII-E, Table 8, pp. 8824-8826)
Limitations / Future Work: Acknowledged challenges: incomplete/noisy multi-vendor telemetry data limiting model accuracy, vendor interoperability gaps, strict real-time latency budgets versus the computational footprint of LLMs and agent workflows, reliability/safety risks including hallucinated configuration commands, compute and token-pricing costs, traceability/transparency for regulated networks, and alignment with operator policies and skills (Sec. VIII, pp. 8827-8830); cited latency gains are "indicative ranges observed in specific implementations rather than universal bounds" (Sec. III-G, p. 8805); future directions: dynamic ecosystems of cooperating agents, telemetry compression (learned encoders, JEPA-style models, semantic tags), distributed DTs, safeguards via causal AI, knowledge graphs, memory-augmented systems and cross-agent validation, multi-vendor telemetry standardization (federated learning, blockchain-style ledgers), and integration with emerging optical fabrics (Sec. IX, Table 11, pp. 8830-8832)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey offers a domain-grounded blueprint of exactly the loop my thesis targets: telemetry/observability as the sensory layer feeding specialized agents (monitoring, fault analysis, planning, execution) whose actions are validated before touching production - a structure directly transferable to an Agentic AI Copilot for incident response, where detection, diagnosis, and remediation agents play analogous roles. Its taxonomy of agentic failure modes and safeguards (stale telemetry, LLM hallucinations, cascading automation errors, human-in-the-loop escalation) informs the safe-autonomy design needed for a copilot intended to reduce MTTD and MTTR. The TM Forum L0-L5 autonomy mapping provides a maturity scale for positioning the copilot's autonomy level. However, as a survey in optical networking without incident-management metrics, it supports conceptual and architectural framing rather than empirical MTTD/MTTR evidence.
Relevance Score: Medium - adjacent work: an observability/AIOps-style architectural survey of telemetry-driven, LLM-enabled multi-agent automation that never measures MTTD or MTTR.

Title: A Neuroergonomics Approach to Mental Workload, Engagement and Human Performance
Authors: Frédéric Dehais; Alex Lafont; Raphaëlle Roy; Stephen Fairclough
Year & Venue: 2020; Frontiers in Neuroscience (Front. Neurosci.), vol. 14, article 268, Neural Technology section; review article; doi: 10.3389/fnins.2020.00268
Core Problem Addressed: Mental workload "remains difficult to operationalize despite decades of research" and the limited-resource metaphor fails to explain critical performance breakdowns of human operators in safety-critical settings (mind wandering, effort withdrawal, perseveration, inattentional blindness/deafness to alarms); the field lacks a framework to predict when operator performance is likely to degrade (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. Introduction / Toward a Limit of the Theory of Limited Resources, pp. 1-3)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No Agentic AI or LLM involved; the paper proposes a neuroergonomic framework mapping undesirable neurocognitive states onto a two-dimensional task engagement x arousal space, monitoring PFC/DLPFC (de)activation via EEG, fNIRS, fMRI, ECG and eye tracking (Table 1), and a closed-loop neuroadaptive-technology pipeline (signal acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, classification, adaptation) triggering three families of countermeasures: (1) user-interface adaptation, (2) task and automation adaptation (dynamic human-automation task reallocation), (3) neuro-adaptation of the end-user (neurofeedback, tDCS) (Sec. Understanding Performance Related Mental States, pp. 5-7; Sec. Solutions to Mitigate Degraded Performance, pp. 7-9)
Methodology: Narrative (non-systematic) literature review with conceptual framework synthesis; maps psycho-physiological and behavioral markers of five degraded mental states in Table 1 and a countermeasure typology in Figure 4; no SLR protocol, dataset, environment, or sample size reported (article type REVIEW, p. 1; Sec. Understanding Performance Related Mental States, pp. 5-8; Sec. Solutions to Mitigate Degraded Performance, pp. 7-10)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — no MTTD, MTTR, or incident-resolution metrics are reported; closest adjacent evidence is cited work on alarm attention: motor-cue pop-up videos "drastically reduced reaction time to alerts during complex situations" and inattentional deafness explains failure to detect auditory alarms (Sec. Adaptation of the User Interface, p. 7; Sec. Understanding Performance Related Mental States, p. 7)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Not applicable for Agentic AI/multi-agent systems; for adaptive automation the review reports cited studies with "better human performance when neuro-adaptive automation was switched on", human-robot authority sharing driven by an online attentional state estimator, and warns that interventions taking over from humans risk "performance impairment and reduced trust in technology" (Sec. Task and Automation Adaptation, pp. 8-9; Sec. Synthesis of Neuro-Adaptive Solutions, p. 9)
Limitations / Future Work: Authors state the framework "remains at the conceptual level and minimizes connections to the complexity of brain functioning"; most neuroadaptive studies are limited to human-machine dyads; long-term efficiency and side effects of tDCS and light exposure require investigation; future work: complex teaming scenarios, hyperscanning, physiological synchrony, collaborative BCIs, and identifying additional degraded mental states and markers (Sec. Conclusion, pp. 10-11; Sec. Neuro-Adaptation of the End-User(s), p. 9)
Relevance to My Thesis: This review grounds the COGNITIVE_LOAD outcome of my RSL: it explains why operator mental workload is hard to operationalize and identifies the degraded states (mind wandering, effort withdrawal, perseveration, inattentional deafness to alarms) that an incident-response copilot should help prevent. Inattentional deafness/blindness to alarms is the neurocognitive substrate of alert fatigue in on-call SRE work, motivating copilots that filter and prioritize alerts. The three-family typology of neuroadaptive countermeasures — especially dynamic task/automation reallocation and the graded escalation from notification to take-over — offers a principled human-in-the-loop design pattern for calibrating an Agentic AI copilot's autonomy level during incidents. Its warning that take-over automation can reduce trust and impair performance informs how much autonomy the copilot should assume. However, it contributes no AIOps, LLM, or MTTD/MTTR evidence.
Relevance Score: Medium — no agentic approach or MTTD/MTTR measurement, but it directly addresses operator cognitive load and human-automation teaming, an adjacent RSL outcome (COGNITIVE_LOAD)

Title: The Chatbot Usability Scale: the Design and Pilot of a Usability Scale for Interaction with AI-Based Conversational Agents
Authors: Simone Borsci; Alessio Malizia; Martin Schmettow; Frank van der Velde; Gunay Tariverdiyeva; Divyaa Balaji; Alan Chamberlain
Year & Venue: 2021 (published online 21 July 2021; issue year 2022); Personal and Ubiquitous Computing (Springer), vol. 26, pp. 95-119
Core Problem Addressed: "Standardised tools to assess a user's satisfaction with the experience of using chatbots and conversational agents are currently unavailable"; existing usability scales (SUS, UMUX, UMUX-LITE) were not developed to consider the conversational aspects that characterise interaction with AI-based CRM chatbots (Abstract; Sec. 1, p. 96)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No agentic framework is proposed; AI-based conversational agents (CRM chatbots) are the object of evaluation, not the solution. Two instruments are developed: (i) BOT-Check, a diagnostic checklist of 14 attributes for short-term CRM agents plus 3 additional attributes for long-term agents, for designers to control chatbot quality; (ii) BUS-15, a 15-item satisfaction questionnaire (5-point Likert) distributed in five factors: perceived accessibility to chatbot functions, perceived quality of chatbot functions, perceived quality of conversation and information provided, perceived privacy and security, and time response (Sec. 5.2.2, p. 108; Sec. 6, p. 109; Appendices 6 and 8)
Methodology: Scale development via four sequential studies: (1) systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines (final database of 34 literature items; revised list of 27 attributes from Radziwill and Benton's 38); (2) online consensus survey with 29 completing participants of 50 invited experts and end-users (Krippendorff's Alpha = 0.780; 17 attributes retained); (3) expert panel (4 members) plus focus groups with 16 volunteers (8 female, 8 male; Age M = 22.1, SD = 2.84) yielding a 42-item BUS over 14 attributes; (4) psychometric pilot with 96 volunteers (22 female, 74 male; Age M = 23.7, SD = 4.8) each interacting with 5 of 10 real CRM chatbots on information-retrieval tasks — 480 questionnaires collected, 385 fully completed — analysed with 50,000-iteration Bayesian Exploratory Factor Analysis (five factors; Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rate = 0.996; items retained with loading over 0.7), reliability analysis, and Pearson correlation with UMUX-LITE on 372 valid measurements (Sec. 2-5, pp. 98-108; Fig. 1, p. 97)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — HCI scale-design and pilot study; no MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or incident resolution time metrics are reported anywhere in the paper (results report only psychometric properties, Sec. 5.2, pp. 108-109)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Not applicable for multi-agent orchestration, autonomy, latency, or cost; for the evaluation of AI-based conversational agents it reports: BUS-15 estimated reliability between .76 and .87 across five factors, overall alpha = .87; BUS-15 satisfaction spanned from a min. of 51.9% to a max. of 80.1% versus 46.8% to 88.1% for UMUX-LITE; the overall BUS-15 strongly correlates with UMUX-LITE per chatbot, while factors F1 (accessibility), F4 (privacy and security) and F5 (time response) capture aspects UMUX-LITE does not (Abstract; Sec. 5.2.2-5.2.3, p. 108; Table 7, p. 106)
Limitations / Future Work: BUS-15 "requires further testing and validation" and "currently cannot be used as an off-the-shelf product for user research and usability tests"; participants were mainly young (below 35 years old) and people with disabilities were not included (attribute 'Meets neurodiverse needs' postponed); further validation is needed with a larger number of chatbots and a more diverse range of participants; some chatbots closed or were suspended during the study (COVID-19), reflecting market volatility (Abstract; Sec. 4.1, p. 105; Sec. 6, p. 109)
Relevance to My Thesis: The paper contains no incident response, AIOps, or observability content, but it provides a piloted instrument (BUS-15) for measuring user satisfaction with AI-based conversational agents. Since the thesis copilot exposes a conversational (LLM-based) interface to SRE/on-call engineers, BUS-15 and its five factors can serve as the human-factors evaluation instrument for operator satisfaction, complementing the objective MTTD/MTTR measurements. The BOT-Check checklist can additionally guide the design and heuristic inspection of the copilot's conversational UX before user testing. The four-study methodology (attribute review, stakeholder consensus, focus groups, psychometric pilot) is also a methodological reference for building operator-facing evaluation questionnaires.
Relevance Score: Low — tangential: it does not measure MTTD/MTTR nor address AIOps or agentic approaches, serving only as a candidate HCI instrument to evaluate satisfaction with the copilot's conversational interface.

Title: WAUC: A Multi-Modal Database for Mental Workload Assessment Under Physical Activity
Authors: Isabela Albuquerque; Abhishek Tiwari; Mark Parent; Raymundo Cassani; Jean-François Gagnon; Daniel Lafond; Sébastien Tremblay; Tiago H. Falk
Year & Venue: 2020; Frontiers in Neuroscience (Front. Neurosci.), vol. 14, article 549524
Core Problem Addressed: Existing objective mental workload (MW) models are trained on static subjects with clinical-grade devices and do not transfer to real-world ambulant operators (e.g., first responders, firefighters, police officers), due to movement artifacts and the interplay between physical activity and MW; to the authors' knowledge no publicly available multi-modal wearable-based dataset existed for MW assessment under physical activity (Sec. 1 and Sec. 2.4, pp. 1-4)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No AI agents, LLMs, or automation frameworks are involved; the contribution is WAUC, an open multi-modal database: 48 participants performed the NASA MATB-II (system monitoring, tracking, resource management) under 2 MW levels (low/high) x 3 physical activity levels (no/medium/high) on a stationary bike or treadmill, with 7 time-synchronized modalities (EEG, ECG, breathing rate, skin temperature, GSR, blood volume pulse, 3-axis accelerometry) recorded via off-the-shelf wearables (Enobio 8-channel EEG headset, Empatica E4 wristband, Zephyr BioHarness3) synchronized with the MuLES software, plus NASA-TLX and Borg fatigue scale subjective ratings; raw data, features, and scripts released at http://musaelab.ca/resources/ (Sec. 1, p. 2; Sec. 3, pp. 4-8)
Methodology: Database/resource paper with a controlled laboratory experiment and validation study; 48 participants (22 treadmill: 9 male/13 female; 26 bike: 16 male/10 female; average age 27.4 ± 6.6 years), full factorial 2 MW x 3 physical strain within-subject design, six 18-min sessions (~2 h total per participant), counterbalanced order; validation via mixed-model repeated-measures ANOVA on NASA-TLX/Borg ratings and binary MW classification with Random Forest (15 estimators) evaluated by AUC under mixed-subjects, intra-subject, and leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (Sec. 3, pp. 4-8; Sec. 4, pp. 8-9)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — no incident-response, MTTD, MTTR, or alert-fatigue metrics are reported; the quantitative results are mental workload classification AUCs (e.g., EEG mixed-subjects AUC 0.945 ± 0.004 under high physical activity; multi-modal fusion cross-subject AUC up to 0.998 ± 0.001; leave-one-subject-out near chance, e.g., 0.500 ± 0.049 for EEG all conditions) (Sec. 5.2-5.4, pp. 9-12)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Not applicable — no agentic or multi-agent system is proposed or evaluated; findings concern human operator monitoring: all subjective ratings were significantly affected by MW manipulation (p < 0.05), physical workload significantly affected all NASA-TLX dimensions except Performance, EEG and breathing features gave the best single-modality performance, multi-modal fusion improved robustness to increased physical workload, and features were not robust to cross-subject variability (Sec. 5, pp. 9-12)
Limitations / Future Work: Achieving state-of-the-art MW prediction was explicitly not a priority ("achieving state-of-the-art MW level prediction performance is not a priority"); leave-one-subject-out classifiers performed poorly, showing features "are not robust to cross-subject variability"; artifact-removal literature is scarce for physiological signals under high physical workload; future directions include studying the physical activity-MW interplay, EEG artifact removal for low-density wearables, detecting MW intensity variations, deep subject-invariant representations, and models adaptive to SNR changes and new subjects (Sec. 4.1, p. 8; Sec. 5.2, p. 10; Sec. 5.5, pp. 12-13)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper contains no Agentic AI, AIOps, or incident-response content and reports no MTTD/MTTR results, so it does not directly inform the copilot architecture of my research. Its value is confined to the RSL Outcome COGNITIVE_LOAD: it operationalizes mental workload measurement through validated subjective instruments (NASA-TLX, Borg scale) and psychophysiological signals from consumer wearables, which could inspire how cognitive load and alert fatigue of on-call SREs are measured when evaluating an Agentic AI copilot during incident response. The finding that MW models generalize poorly across subjects is a caution for any operator-state monitoring component. Overall it is background material on workload measurement methodology rather than evidence for the thesis's core questions.
Relevance Score: Low — the study is tangential: it provides a mental workload assessment database with no agentic/AI incident-response approach and no MTTD/MTTR measurement, relating to the thesis only via the COGNITIVE_LOAD outcome instruments.

Title: From Vulnerability to Defense: The Role of Large Language Models in Enhancing Cybersecurity
Authors: Wafaa Kasri; Yassine Himeur; Hamzah Ali Alkhazaleh; Saed Tarapiah; Shadi Atalla; Wathiq Mansoor; Hussain Al-Ahmad
Core Problem Addressed: The escalating complexity of cyber threats and rapidly evolving digital landscapes outpace traditional cybersecurity mechanisms, which "often fall short in detecting, mitigating, and responding to complex risks"; the review targets how LLMs can address these gaps across threat detection, phishing, malware analysis, and incident response (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, pp. 1-2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Review article — no single system is proposed; it surveys LLMs (GPT, BERT, PaLM, T5, etc.) applied to threat identification, phishing/malware/intrusion detection, vulnerability management, threat intelligence, incident response, cloud security, compliance and endpoint security, and distills generic LLM-based frameworks (Algorithms 1-3) for malware detection, intrusion detection, and cloud security; agentic elements appear in surveyed works: multi-agent Audit-LLM for insider threat detection, multi-agent AutoDefense against jailbreaks, an LLM agent framework for dynamic phishing detection, and AIOps-style incident systems (Xpert, IcM BRAIN, RCACopilot, IncidentResponseGPT); future integration of LLMs with SOAR platforms is proposed for automated incident response with human analysts in the loop (Sec. 3, pp. 10-33; Sec. 3.7, p. 25; Sec. 5.3, p. 39; Sec. 8.2, p. 46)
Methodology: Narrative/critical literature review with taxonomy: structured by application domain (Fig. 1), with 14 comparative tables of primary studies (models, datasets, contributions, best performance, limitations), a taxonomy table (Table 12), case studies, and three step-by-step LLM frameworks (Algorithms 1-3); no SLR protocol (e.g., PRISMA), search strategy, or count of reviewed studies is reported; no own dataset or experiments (Sec. 1, pp. 2-3; Fig. 1, p. 4; Sec. 4, pp. 34-35)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: No MTTD/MTTR measurements are reported (review paper); qualitative claims only: LLM log analysis "not only improves detection accuracy but also reduces response times" and incident documentation "streamlines incident management and minimizes response delays" (Sec. 2.3.1, p. 6); DrSec reduces alert fatigue, achieving 75.11% PR AUC in alert triage (Sec. 3.11, pp. 31-32); a surveyed LLM recommender for support requests aims "to reduce mean resolution times" with no figures given (Sec. 3.9, p. 29); surveyed incident-management results: 95.2% accuracy in traffic-incident severity classification, 87% accuracy in ticket categorization, 92% efficiency in resource allocation (Table 7, p. 25); RCACopilot automates root cause analysis with RCA accuracy of 0.766 (Sec. 3.9, p. 28)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Surveyed multi-agent results: Audit-LLM (multi-agent framework with COT reasoning) is "superior to existing baselines" for insider threat detection but suffers "faithfulness hallucination in LLM conclusions" (Sec. 3.10, p. 30; Table 10, p. 30); a multi-agent defense framework collaboratively filters harmful LLM responses, with effectiveness "dependent on the division and coordination of tasks" (Sec. 5.3, p. 39; Table 13, p. 38); an LLM agent framework that dynamically fetches online information for phishing detection reached 94.5% accuracy but depends on external data fetching (Sec. 3.2, p. 13; Table 2, p. 14); the conclusion flags "collaborative multi-agent systems" as an emerging research direction (Sec. 9, p. 48)
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations of LLMs (not of the review itself): interpretability ("black boxes"), lack of domain-specific knowledge, scalability/computational cost, adversarial attacks, plus ethical issues of bias, privacy, misuse, and accountability (Sec. 5.6-5.7, pp. 41-43); deployment challenges: data privacy/memorization, integration with SIEM/IDS/SOAR infrastructures, robustness to prompt injection, contextual accuracy ("faithfulness"), real-time scalability, and catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (Sec. 7, pp. 44-46); future directions: LLM detection of social engineering, automation of incident responses via SOAR integration, disruption of phishing campaigns, and tailored security education programs (Sec. 8, pp. 46-47)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey is a useful secondary source that maps the LLM-for-security landscape, including a dedicated incident response and management section covering AIOps-adjacent systems (Xpert for KQL query recommendation, IcM BRAIN, RCACopilot, IncidentResponseGPT) that automate triage, root cause analysis, and response planning — the same operational stages where my thesis targets MTTD/MTTR reduction. Its explicit future direction of coupling LLMs with SOAR platforms and playbook-driven response mirrors the copilot role of my proposed Agentic AI. It also aggregates evidence on multi-agent frameworks (Audit-LLM, AutoDefense) and their failure modes (faithfulness hallucination, coordination dependence), which informs my architecture risks. However, it is cybersecurity-centric and reports no MTTD/MTTR quantification, so it serves as background and a citation hub rather than as empirical evidence for my metrics.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent: a broad LLM-in-cybersecurity survey that covers incident response automation, AIOps-style systems, and multi-agent frameworks, but measures no MTTD/MTTR with an agentic approach

Title: Breaking Alert Fatigue: AI-Assisted SIEM Framework for Effective Incident Response
Authors: Tao Ban; Takeshi Takahashi; Samuel Ndichu; Daisuke Inoue
Year & Venue: 2023; Applied Sciences (Appl. Sci.), MDPI, vol. 13, article 6610
Core Problem Addressed: Contemporary SIEM solutions struggle to identify critical security incidents because of the overwhelming number of false alerts generated by disparate security products (IDSs), causing alert fatigue that desensitizes SOC analysts, delays incident responses, and leads to overlooked critical incidents (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Next-generation SIEM framework integrating SOAR capabilities with a divide-and-conquer strategy splitting alert fatigue into a filtering problem and a correlation problem; four modules (alert generation, feature processing with CEF-to-JSON unification and one-hot encoding, ML, investigation); filtering via IWSVM (instance-weighted SVM, cost-sensitive learning combining class and instance weights, LIBSVM solver); correlation via an entropy-based event segmenting algorithm grouping alerts by three-tuple [source IP, destination IP, service port] plus timeout (tau=7200 s, beta=0.58); augmented tile graph (ATG) visualization to expedite triage; human-in-the-loop: SOC personnel label alerts and AI experts validate labels via visualization; no LLM or agentic component (Sec. 3, pp. 6-10; Sec. 4, pp. 10-14)
Methodology: Empirical experimental evaluation (prototype of key components) on real-world alert logs from a class-B enterprise network with over 1000 users and 30,000 network devices; two datasets: NSOC2017 (six IDSs, 1 Jan-31 Oct 2017; 137.77 M total alerts per Table 2, stated as 133.77 million in the text, 593 escalations; after subsampling 2239 positive and 672,000 negative samples, 0.333% positive ratio) and NSOC2022 (two appliances, 18 Jun 2021-30 Nov 2022, 7.3 million alert log lines); five-fold stratified cross validation (SCV) and rolling origin validation (ROV); metrics: accuracy, recall, precision, FPR, TNR, F1, BCR, ARR, GARR; parameter tuning via 10-fold SCV in MATLAB (Sec. 5, pp. 16-22)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD/MTTR not measured; alert-fatigue results: IWSVM achieved best filtering on NSOC2017 with Recall 99.643%, Precision 99.687%, FPR 0.001%, F1 99.665% (Table 3, p. 20); on NSOC2022 under ROV, F1 over 99.3% in all settings (Table 5, p. 21); on the preliminary escalation set, Alert Reduction Rate (ARR) of 45.850%, 45.010%, 49.400%, 50.490%, and 47.470% across settings 1-5 ("close to or greater than a 50% ARR value") (Table 6, p. 22); combining filtering and correlation, GARR of 74.070% to 83.980% — "reduced the alert volume by nearly or greater than 75%" — with events to investigate cut to 1512 down to 206 per interval (Table 7, Sec. 5.5.2, p. 22)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Not applicable — the framework uses conventional supervised ML (cost-sensitive IWSVM), clustering/segmentation heuristics, and visualization rather than agentic or multi-agent AI; SOAR automation is rule/playbook-based, and the authors note SOAR research is still at an early stage requiring further work on orchestration and incident response automation (Sec. 2.1.3, p. 4; Sec. 3, p. 6)
Limitations / Future Work: Scope limited to eliminating redundant/irrelevant alerts; results biased by the specific SOC's escalation set, security policy, and analyst condition (including alert fatigue during labeling); eliminating all false positives risks increased false negatives (recommend recall threshold such as 99%); emerging threats and adversarial attacks can cause false negatives; detection performance degrades as the train-test interval grows, requiring regular model updates; future work: pilot study with industry partners in a real-world SOC, scalability assessment, and evaluation on larger datasets covering more attack types and network environments (Sec. 6, pp. 22-24)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper quantifies the alert-fatigue problem that inflates MTTD/MTTR in SOCs and demonstrates that AI-assisted filtering plus correlation can safely remove roughly 75-84% of alert volume before human triage, a concrete baseline for what pre-LLM, non-agentic AIOps achieves. Its divide-and-conquer decomposition (filtering vs. correlation) and its metrics (ARR, GARR, recall-first thresholds) are directly reusable to evaluate an Agentic AI copilot's triage stage. The human-in-the-loop labeling and SOAR integration points map to where an agentic copilot could replace static playbooks. As a non-agentic contrast case, it helps position the thesis gap: high filtering accuracy is achievable, but investigation and response remain manual, which is precisely where an Agentic AI copilot targets MTTD/MTTR.
Relevance Score: Medium — directly addresses alert fatigue and SOC triage efficiency with AI (adjacent AIOps theme) but has no agentic/LLM component and does not measure MTTD or MTTR.

Title: Transitioning from MLOps to LLMOps: Navigating the Unique Challenges of Large Language Models
Authors: Pahune, Saurabh; Akhtar, Zahid
Core Problem Addressed: Many ML applications fail to reach production, and traditional MLOps techniques do not fully address the unique operational challenges of LLMs — scalability, security, ethical considerations, and infrastructure requirements; the authors note that "the industry currently prioritizes MLOps but ignores LLMOps" and that gaps remain in addressing LLM challenges (Sec. 1, pp. 1-3).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No agentic system is proposed; the paper is a review that characterizes LLMOps as a specialized subcategory of MLOps, describing an LLMOps architecture pattern based on RAG (user prompt -> embedding model -> vector database -> context augmentation -> LLM output), the 4D lifecycle framework (Discover, Distill, Deploy, Deliver), Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) oversight, and comparative evaluations of platforms such as LangChain, Hugging Face Transformers, DeepSpeed, Vertex AI, and Azure Bot Service with OpenAI (Sec. 3.2, pp. 10-11; Sec. 3.4, pp. 12-13; Sec. 3.6, pp. 15-16).

The RAG architecture pattern and the platform comparisons (LangChain, Vertex AI) inform concrete implementation choices for the copilot prototype. Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent work: it covers LLM operations (LLMOps) and touches AIOps, but proposes no agentic incident-response approach and reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements.

Title: Toward Robust Security Orchestration and Automated Response in Security Operations Centers with a Hyper-Automation Approach Using Agentic Artificial Intelligence
Authors: Ismail; Rahmat Kurnia; Zilmas Arjuna Brata; Ghitha Afina Nelistiani; Shinwook Heo; Hyeongon Kim; Howon Kim
Core Problem Addressed: Traditional no-code/low-code SOAR platforms in SOCs face restricted flexibility, scalability challenges, inadequate support for advanced logic, and difficulty managing large playbooks, which hinders effective automation, reduces adaptability, and underutilizes analysts' technical expertise while SOC teams are overwhelmed by rising alert volume and complexity (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 1).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A hyper-automation SOAR platform powered by agentic-LLM that shifts from rigid no-code playbooks to AI-generated code, plus the IVAM framework (Investigation, Validation, Active Monitoring) integrating MITRE ATT&CK, NIST CSF, and Quantitative Risk Assessment (QRA); three-layer multi-agent architecture: (i) planning/data management with a Vector DB for incident similarity retrieval, (ii) model orchestration with an Agent Router over two LLMs (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct for broad security policy and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B for deep domain-specific analysis), (iii) tooling/execution with a Technical Step Builder, a human_interrupt_node for human-in-the-loop review/approval, and a WebSocket Agent Client for remote command execution; flow logic implemented as a state transition graph of modular nodes (router, incident similarity, problem extraction, technical steps, script capture, executor, report) (Sec. 3.1, p. 10; Sec. 3.2, pp. 15-19; Sec. 3.4, pp. 22-24).
Methodology: Prototype pilot deployment in a controlled SOC-like virtualized environment (VirtualBox on Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, 13th-gen Intel Core i7 host) integrated with the Wazuh SIEM, using an SSH brute-force attack proof-of-concept as the use case; the agent-generated mitigation (ten actions) was qualitatively compared against the Cortex XSOAR "Brute-Force Investigation—Generic" playbook (38 steps); QRA applied incrementally per mitigation step; MTTR measured over three remediation activities; no sample size beyond the single use case reported (Sec. 4.1, p. 25; Sec. 4.3, pp. 26-28; Sec. 4.4, p. 28; Sec. 4.6, p. 30).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD: Not specified. MTTR (defined here as Mean Time to Remediate) measured across three remediation activities: analysis "approximately 1 min and 30 s on average", update command execution "around 1 min", compilation "approximately 1 min and 30 s"; comparison is against the literature (a referenced Microsoft Copilot for Security study [83]), NOT an own baseline: the referenced platforms averaged "approximately 45 s" for analysis and compilation and "around 30 s" for command updates, i.e., the proposed system was slower, and the authors state closed access to alternative-platform data prevented direct comparative analysis; additionally, the AI agent condensed the 38-step XSOAR playbook into ten key actions; Sec. 4.1 (p. 25) frames Mean Time to Respond (MTTR) benchmarking as future work, indicating internal terminology inconsistency (Sec. 4.6, p. 30; Sec. 4.3, p. 26; Sec. 4.1, p. 25).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: The pilot "successfully processed real-time security alerts and autonomously executed mitigation workflows without human intervention", providing empirical evidence of operational viability of an autonomous agent-based SOAR architecture; workflow condensation from 38 XSOAR steps to ten actions with more granular tool recommendations (Fail2Ban, AIDE, auditd, Google Authenticator MFA); adaptive error resolution demonstrated a failure mode: repeated sudo-password authentication failures led the agent to iterate diagnostics over 5 steps and issue a Human Intervention Request (Table 3); QRA showed "a measurable reduction in security risk at each stage of the response lifecycle"; noted autonomy constraints include limited access to agentless OT devices and WebSocket-based active response (Sec. 4.1, p. 25; Sec. 4.3, p. 26; Sec. 4.5, pp. 29-30; Sec. 5, p. 31).
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: risk of misclassification/false positives requiring human validation; effectiveness depends on quality/completeness of training data; interpretability and trust of AI-generated recommendations; integration with third-party tools; limited direct access to agentless devices such as OT systems; constraints of WebSocket-based active responses; validation "remains limited in scope" (single brute-force use case); restricted/closed access to alternative-platform remediation data limited the MTTR comparison. Future work: continuous learning and validation against real-world attack datasets; improved explainability and human-in-the-loop validation; broader validation strategies across diverse environments; extension to phishing detection, privilege escalation, and ransomware mitigation; collection of quantitative metrics (MTTR, mitigation success rate, reduction in analyst intervention) benchmarked against conventional SOAR platforms (Sec. 5, p. 31; Sec. 6, p. 31; Sec. 4.6, p. 30; Sec. 4.1, p. 25).
Relevance to My Thesis: Highly relevant: it presents a full agentic-LLM incident-response pipeline (multi-agent orchestration, vector-memory retrieval, human-in-the-loop approval) that operates as a SOC copilot, matching the thesis architecture space. It is one of the few primary studies reporting concrete measured MTTR values for an agentic approach, and its result — slower than the Microsoft Copilot for Security literature reference — is a valuable cautionary datapoint that agentic autonomy can carry latency costs. The IVAM framework and per-step QRA offer a reusable structure for validating copilot actions and quantifying risk reduction during response. Its gaps map directly onto the thesis opportunity: MTTD is not measured, and the MTTR comparison lacks an own controlled baseline, motivating a design with proper before/after MTTD-MTTR measurement.
Relevance Score: High — it directly measures MTTR with an agentic-LLM multi-agent SOAR approach in an incident-response pilot (though MTTD is not measured and the MTTR comparison is against literature rather than an own baseline).
