Title: Advancing Cyber Incident Timeline Analysis Through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Models
Authors: Fatma Yasmine Loumachi; Mohamed Chahine Ghanem; Mohamed Amine Ferrag
Core Problem Addressed: Cyber/forensic timeline analysis in DFIR investigations is time-consuming due to the volume and heterogeneity of artefacts and the reliance on multiple specialised standalone tools; existing solutions present final timelines without sufficient semantic context (only timestamps are correlated) and make it difficult to spot and extract evidence supporting root-cause claims (Sec. 1 and Research Question, pp. 2-3).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: GenDFIR, an LLM-powered framework integrating Llama 3.1 8B in zero-shot with a DFIR context-specific RAG agent (Autonomous Context-Augmented Agent); stage 1 preprocesses incident events (CSV artefacts) into a structured textual knowledge base with event-level chunking; stage 2 embeds events and the DFIR expert's query with mxbai-embed-large, retrieves top-k relevant events via cosine similarity, applies agent-role contextual filtering and attention-based enrichment, and a decoder-based LLM generates a human-readable timeline analysis report; human-in-the-loop design: the DFIR expert's query drives evidence identification and human verification at key stages is stated as essential (Sec. 3, pp. 9-18; Sec. 4.1, pp. 20-21; Sec. 5.2, p. 30).
Methodology: Prototype implementation with controlled experiment on 6 synthetic cyber incident scenarios (SYN Flood, 30 events; Rhino Hunt, 8; Phishing Email-1, 15; Phishing Email-2, 20; DNS Spoof, 23; Unauthorised Access, 25), all run locally (Python/PyTorch, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 8 GB VRAM, CUDA 12.6; temperature = 0.1, max tokens = 2000, n = 1); outputs evaluated with DFIR-tailored metrics (accuracy, relevance, exact match, top-k evidence retrieval) cross-referenced against the ground-truth knowledge base, supported by human evaluation; 20 relevance prompts per scenario (240 prompts in total on the project repository) (Sec. 4.2-4.3, pp. 21-22; Sec. 5.2, pp. 23-29).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — MTTD/MTTR are not measured; only a qualitative claim that GenDFIR leverages the LLM's contextual understanding to "accelerate and improve incident analysis, minimising reliance on manual intervention" (Sec. 3.4, p. 17); motivation cites investigators spending an average of 45 h per case on digital evidence examination (Sec. 1, p. 2); framework performance instead reported as Accuracy 95.52%, Relevance 94.51%, EM 100%, Top-K 100%, Overall 97.51% (Table 8, p. 32).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: A single autonomous LLM-powered RAG agent (not multi-agent) achieved 97.51% overall performance across the tailored metrics; observed failure modes include a fabricated timestamp (04:30 p.m.) in the Phishing Email-1 report and failed/partial answers on some relevance prompts (e.g., SYN Flood Prompt 4; Rhino Hunt Prompt 13 at 50%); tool comparison shows GenDFIR as the only one producing a full contextual timeline report vs. Splunk, FTK/Autopsy, Velociraptor and Timesketch; authors state LLMs "should not be regarded as fully autonomous systems" and plan specialised autonomous LLM agents per task (Sec. 5.2, pp. 24-25; Tables 8-9, p. 32; Sec. 6.2, p. 35; Sec. 6.3, p. 36).
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: novelty of applying LLMs to timeline analysis (few guidelines/benchmarks); synthetic, simplified scenarios excluding anti-forensics techniques; data volume/heterogeneity and scalability challenges (token limits, hardware); privacy and data-security constraints (GDPR, NIS2); evaluation methods still manual and deemed insufficient by the authors; Future work: integrate real-world incident data, implement specialised autonomous LLM agents for timeline analysis, evidence correlation and root-cause identification, develop novel evaluation metrics, deploy larger models with higher token limits, and extend to IoT security, regulatory compliance and legal proceedings (Sec. 6.1, pp. 33-35; Sec. 6.3, p. 36).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper offers a concrete, reproducible architecture (zero-shot LLM + context-specific RAG agent + knowledge-base retrieval) for automating incident event correlation and timeline reconstruction, a task directly analogous to what an Agentic AI copilot must do during incident response. Its qualitative claim of accelerating analysis and minimising manual intervention aligns with the MTTD/MTTR-reduction goal, although the paper never operationalises those metrics. The DFIR-tailored evaluation protocol (accuracy, relevance, exact match, top-k evidence against a ground-truth knowledge base, with human verification) is a useful template for assessing copilot output reliability in my experiments. The documented failure modes (hallucinated timestamp, partial answers) and the human-in-the-loop stance inform the copilot's autonomy-level design. Its focus is DFIR forensics rather than SRE/AIOps operations, so transfer requires adaptation.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent work: a single-agent RAG/LLM framework that automates incident timeline analysis and qualitatively claims faster investigations, but does not measure MTTD/MTTR.

Title: AI-Augmented SOC: A Survey of LLMs and Agents for Security Automation
Authors: Siddhant Srinivas; Brandon Kirk; Julissa Zendejas; Michael Espino; Matthew Boskovich; Abdul Bari; Khalil Dajani; Nabeel Alzahrani
Year & Venue: 2025; Journal of Cybersecurity and Privacy (J. Cybersecur. Priv., MDPI), vol. 5, art. 95; DOI 10.3390/jcp5040095
Core Problem Addressed: Traditional rule-based and manual SOC processes are insufficient against the growing volume, velocity, and sophistication of cyber threats, leading to alert fatigue, delayed responses, high false-positive rates, analyst dependency, and escalating operational costs; prior surveys on LLMs for cyber defense remain domain-specific and fragmented, lacking a unified, SOC-centered operational synthesis (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No new system; the survey contributes (i) an integrated taxonomy of LLM and AI-agent applications across eight SOC tasks (log summarization, alert triage, threat intelligence, ticket handling, incident response, report generation, asset discovery and management, vulnerability management), in which AI agents orchestrate data collection, tool use, memory, and planning while LLMs (GPT-3.5/4/4o, LLaMA, Claude, Gemini, Mistral, BERT variants) serve as the cognitive backbone, spanning autonomous vs. human-in-the-loop modes (Sec. 3, pp. 3-10; Tables 1-2, pp. 4, 11); and (ii) a five-level capability-maturity model (Manual -> AI/LLM-Assisted -> Semi-Autonomous -> Conditionally Autonomous -> Fully Autonomous) using HITL/HoTL/HoOTL designs, positioned as an AI-focused overlay to SOC-CMM (Sec. 4, pp. 12-13)
Methodology: ⚠ Ambiguous: reported screening counts do not reconcile arithmetically (510 screened; 300 eliminated; 105 included). Systematic literature review (survey) following PRISMA 2020, preregistered at OSF (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/9QC7V); initial pool of over 600 papers (2022-2025, last searched 15 July 2025) from IEEE Xplore, arXiv, ACM Digital Library, and proceedings of NDSS, USENIX Security, ACM CCS, and IEEE S&P, including peer-reviewed and preprint sources; after preliminary screening of 510 papers and elimination of 300 for lack of SOC relevance, 105 papers were each independently reviewed by four authors against explicit inclusion criteria; disagreements resolved by consensus (Sec. 2, pp. 2-3; Sec. 7, p. 19)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Secondary evidence only (survey reports results of cited primary studies; no own measurements): CyberAlly's AI-driven triage "halved false positives from 70% to 35% and reduced Mean Time To Respond (MTTR) from 8 h to 90 min", with automated ticketing rising from 10% to 75% (Sec. 3.2, p. 6); alert-fatigue baseline: SOCs process over 10,000 daily alerts, more than half false positives (Sec. 3.2, p. 5); breach baseline of 204 days to identify plus 73 days to contain (277 days total) (Sec. 3.5, p. 7); ReliaQuest GreyMatter processes alerts 20 times faster, automates 98% of alerts, and reduces containment time to under 5 min (Sec. 3.7, p. 9); Microsoft CTI framework cuts report generation time from 8 h to under 2 h (Sec. 3.6, pp. 8-9); AGIR reduces report writing time by 42.6% and TickIt reduces alerts by 30% (Sec. 3.6, p. 8; Sec. 3.4, p. 7); Table 2 cites 6x faster detection/mitigation and task completion time down 30.69% for IT Admins (Table 2, p. 11); projection: AI agents expected to significantly reduce MTTD and MTTM, with simulations up to six times faster response than human intervention (Sec. 6, p. 18)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Across all eight SOC tasks, AI-augmented systems consistently improve detection accuracy, reduce false positives, and accelerate response over rule-based methods, but current implementations largely remain at maturity Levels 1-2 with human oversight (Sec. 8, pp. 19-20); multi-agent results: TrioXpert improves anomaly detection 4.7-57.7%, failure triage 2.1-40.6%, root cause localization 1.6-163.1%, with average end-to-end diagnosis within 15 s (Sec. 3.5, p. 8); IRCopilot achieves sub-task completion rates up to 150% higher than directly applying GPT-4 (Sec. 3.5, p. 8); Audit-LLM shows 40% false-positive reduction for insider threat detection (Sec. 6, pp. 17-18); cost evidence: CTINEXUS full experiment under $0.30, LLexus about $0.5 per incident (~50,000 tokens) (Sec. 3.3, p. 6; Sec. 3.4, p. 7); failure modes: communication overhead and scalability bottlenecks, emergent behaviors hindering predictability, Agent-in-the-Middle attacks, prompt injection, memory poisoning, hallucination cascades, and data leakage (Sec. 5-5.1, pp. 14-15; Table 4, pp. 14-15)
Limitations / Future Work: Five stated threats to validity: selection bias (post-2022, English-only filtering), ecological validity (most studies use simulated/benchmarked environments, so metrics may not extrapolate to operational SOCs), measurement inconsistency (heterogeneous metrics and datasets hinder cross-comparison), evolving baselines (findings are a snapshot prone to obsolescence), and human-AI integration uncertainty (few empirical studies of human-AI collaboration at scale) (Sec. 7, p. 19); the capability-maturity model is not yet validated — future multi-phase validation should correlate maturity scores with MTTD, MTTR, and false-positive rates (Sec. 4.2, p. 13); future directions include XAI, RLHF, standardized adversarial benchmarks (ASB), privacy-preserving models, and empirical testing in operational SOC environments (Sec. 6, pp. 17-18; Sec. 8, p. 20)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey maps almost one-to-one onto the thesis topic: it synthesizes how LLM-based copilots and agentic/multi-agent systems augment SOC incident response, the same operational setting where the thesis proposes an Agentic AI Copilot to reduce MTTD and MTTR. Its eight-task taxonomy and five-level capability-maturity model provide a ready framework for positioning the copilot's autonomy level (HITL/HoTL) and for structuring related work. It consolidates secondary MTTR and alert-fatigue evidence (e.g., CyberAlly 8 h -> 90 min MTTR; GreyMatter containment under 5 min; 277-day breach baseline) that can serve as reference baselines, and its proposed model validation explicitly adopts MTTD/MTTR as performance indicators — the exact metrics of the thesis. The catalogued incident-response copilots (IRCopilot, AidAI, TrioXpert) and the identified gaps (ecological validity, lack of operational human-AI studies) directly motivate the thesis's empirical contribution.
Relevance Score: High — although a secondary study, it directly surveys agentic AI/LLM copilots for SOC incident response, consolidates MTTD/MTTR/alert-fatigue evidence, and offers a maturity framework and gap analysis immediately applicable to the thesis.

Title: Enhancing Control Room Operator Decision Making
Authors: Joseph Mietkiewicz; Ammar N. Abbas; Chidera W. Amazu; Gabriele Baldissone; Anders L. Madsen; Micaela Demichela; Maria Chiara Leva
Core Problem Addressed: Control room operators in industrial (chemical) plants are inundated with tasks and alerts, leading to task overload, decision fatigue and reliance on cognitive biases that compromise decision making during critical process disturbances; DSSs for such safety-critical settings must be effective yet interpretable and trustworthy (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 2). Note: the problem domain is industrial process control, not IT operations/SRE.
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: AI-based DSS framework called "Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence for Safety-Critical Systems" (HAISC): a dynamic influence diagram (DID; Bayesian-network-based, built in HUGIN software from expert knowledge and physical process equations) detects anomalies via conflict analysis, forecasts states over 10 one-minute time slices and recommends maximum-expected-utility actions; localized deep RL agents (TD3-based, in a multi-specialized reinforcement learning agent (M-SRLA) setup where multiple agents run independently and a specific agent is activated when the DID detects an abnormality) refine interval recommendations into precise continuous values, accepted only if inside the DID-recommended interval — otherwise the interpretable DID suggestion takes precedence; the model operates within a human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework assisting, not replacing, the operator (Sec. 3.2, p. 18; Algorithm 1, p. 19; Sec. 3.1.5, p. 17).
Methodology: Controlled between-subjects experiment in a simulated formaldehyde-production control room (production of 10,000 kg/h of 30% formaldehyde solution; 80 alarms of different priority levels incl. nuisance alarms; 3 fault scenarios); 48 volunteer participants, predominantly chemical-engineering master's students: Group G1 without DSS n=23, Group G2 with DSS n=25; measures: SART and SPAM for situation awareness, NASA TLX for workload, reaction time / response time / overall performance from operational data (21 participants per group), smartwatch physiological data — heart rate, temperature, EDA (G1 n=14, G2 n=17); statistics: Shapiro–Wilk, Levene's test, Student's/Welch's T-test, Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann–Whitney U (p < 0.05) (Sec. 2.1, p. 5; Sec. 2.5, p. 13; Sec. 4, pp. 21–26).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable for MTTD/MTTR as such (industrial control-room study, not IT incident response); analogous time-to-detect/act metrics improved with the DSS: mean reaction time S1 106.96 (G2) vs 276.30 (G1), S2 63.43 vs 266.91, S3 117.38 vs 190.17; mean response time S1 259.04 vs 339.30, S2 154.83 vs 361.48, S3 680.00 vs 787.87 (units not stated in Table 5); Wilcoxon tests show significant differences except in scenario 3 (reaction time p=0.00 S1/S2 vs 0.14 S3; overall performance p=0.00/0.05/1.00); frustration (NASA TLX) significantly lower with DSS (p=0.04/0.02) while overall TLX index showed no significant difference (Sec. 4.4, Tables 4–5, pp. 25–26; Sec. 4.3, Table 3, p. 24).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Demonstrates a hierarchical HITL architecture in which multiple specialized RL agents function independently and only the relevant agent is activated upon DID-detected anomaly (M-SRLA); safety guardrail: the black-box RL continuous value is used only if it falls within the interpretable DID's recommended interval (e.g., in scenario 1 the RL agent suggested 5.6 m3/h inside the DID range 4–7 m3/h); trade-off uncovered: the DSS group showed significantly lower situation awareness (SPAM index, monitoring and intervention, p=0.00), attributed to possible over-reliance on the system's guidance, while heart rate was borderline lower with DSS (Welch p=0.05) (Sec. 3.2, p. 18; Sec. 3.3, pp. 19–20; Sec. 4.2, Table 2, pp. 22–23; Sec. 4.5, Table 6, p. 26; Sec. 5.2, p. 29).
Limitations / Future Work: Scalability: constructing a DID covering the entire process from physical equations is challenging and time-intensive, forcing focus on parts of the plant or more generic models/recommendations; participants were mostly chemical-engineering students who "lack real-world experience as control room operators"; physiological data analyzed raw, without accounting for individual differences; DID discretization trades precision against unwieldy CPT size and high computational time; future work: optimize discretization and model complexity, revise CPTs (including integrating empirical data), and add a "What If" display of consequences of recommended actions (Sec. 5.1, pp. 28–29; Sec. 5.3, pp. 29–30).
Relevance to My Thesis: Although set in an industrial control room rather than IT operations, this paper empirically validates the exact HITL pattern my thesis proposes: an AI copilot that detects anomalies and recommends actions while the human operator keeps decision authority. Its evidence that AI decision support significantly cuts reaction and response times to faults parallels the MTTD/MTTR reductions I target in incident response, and the reduced frustration and heart rate speak directly to alert fatigue and operator cognitive load. The measured trade-off — lower situation awareness from over-reliance on the system — is a key design caution for an incident-response copilot that must keep the on-call engineer engaged. Finally, its guardrail pattern (black-box RL output accepted only within an interpretable model's safe interval) is transferable to safe agentic automation in production environments.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent: it empirically measures human-in-the-loop AI decision support with time-to-react/respond gains and cognitive-workload effects, but in industrial process control rather than IT incident response, and it does not report MTTD/MTTR.

Title: Artificial Intelligence Agent-Enabled Predictive Maintenance: Conceptual Proposal and Basic Framework
Authors: Wenyu Jiang; Fuwen Hu
Core Problem Addressed: Successful deployment of predictive maintenance (PdM) systems is hindered by intertwined challenges — system integration complexity, data quality and data availability, interdisciplinary talent gaps, high initial investment, and operational fragmentation — while traditional PdM relies heavily on single models and static rules (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: An AI agent-enabled PdM method that combines "AI workflow + large reasoning models + operational knowledge base + digital twin" with BaaS and LLMOps concepts into an end-to-end closed loop from data perception to decision execution; four core agents (diagnostic, scheduling, summing-up/evaluation, and digital twin fault handling simulation) collaborate via a message-driven workflow over a three-tier edge–fog–cloud architecture; technology stack: Dify (low-code workflow engine), RAGFlow (RAG knowledge base), DeepSeek (LLM reasoning), AutoGen multi-agent planners at the fog tier, plus MCP and A2A protocols for interoperability (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 3, pp. 6–8; Sec. 4.1, pp. 8–10)
Methodology: Conceptual proposal: a reference architecture, an exploratory implementation roadmap, and a proof-of-concept prototype demo of agentic AI-based PdM for wind turbine rolling bearings built on Dify with the RAGFlow knowledge base, DeepSeek reasoning, and simulated equipment sensor data and enterprise resource data; no empirical evaluation, real dataset, or sample size reported (Sec. 4.1, pp. 8–10; Sec. 4.2, pp. 10–11)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — no MTTD, MTTR, or incident-resolution-time metrics are measured; the framework only qualitatively targets minimizing downtime and preventing secondary failures, and the sole quantitative figure is that in the roadmap trained classifiers "detect anomalies (e.g., abnormal vibration thresholds) with 95% accuracy" (Sec. 4.1, p. 9; Sec. 3.4, p. 8)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Proposes a tiered L1/L2/L3 agent development paradigm (low-code platforms, API-driven tools, full-code frameworks) that lowers entry barriers; four-agent separation of concerns with message-driven collaboration and a continuous learning loop; RAG mitigates hallucinations and digital twins pre-test maintenance actions for decision reliability; prototyping indicates that "Dify reduces LLM app development from weeks to hours"; MCP/A2A protocols cited as enablers for scalable industrial AI agents — all claims are conceptual, without measured efficacy, latency, or cost (Sec. 2.1, pp. 4–5; Sec. 4.2, p. 10; Sec. 4.3, p. 12; Sec. 5, p. 12)
Limitations / Future Work: Authors state the work "remains a high-level architectural proposal" without evidence that the intricate system would outperform simpler approaches; dependence on high-quality sensor data and historical fault records; challenges in cross-factory distributed collaboration under privacy constraints; optimization hurdles for edge deployment in resource-constrained environments; future work: synthetic data generation via physics-based models, federated learning for secure multi-factory knowledge sharing, edge-optimized algorithms, and standardized multi-agent communication protocols (Sec. 5, pp. 12–13)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper offers a transferable architectural blueprint for the thesis: its four-agent pipeline (detection → diagnosis → action planning → feedback learning) mirrors the incident response lifecycle underlying MTTD and MTTR, and its "multi-agent + RAG + reasoning engine + digital twin" closed loop parallels an Agentic AI copilot orchestrating observability data and runbooks. The tiered L1/L2/L3 development paradigm and the Dify/RAGFlow/DeepSeek stack inform practical build choices for a copilot prototype, and the use of RAG to mitigate hallucinations addresses a key reliability concern for LLM-based incident assistants. However, the domain is industrial equipment maintenance rather than IT operations, and the absence of any MTTD/MTTR-style measurement means the paper contributes design patterns, not evidence, to the thesis
Relevance Score: Low — tangential: a conceptual multi-agent PdM framework for industrial equipment, outside IT incident response and without any MTTD/MTTR measurement, contributing only transferable orchestration patterns

Title: Enhancing Security Operations Center: Wazuh Security Event Response with Retrieval-Augmented-Generation-Driven Copilot
Authors: Ismail; Rahmat Kurnia; Farid Widyatama; Ilham Mirwansyah Wibawa; Zilmas Arjuna Brata; Ukasyah; Ghitha Afina Nelistiani; Howon Kim
Core Problem Addressed: SOCs face shortage of skilled personnel, limited automation, process-integration inconsistencies, and SIEM-induced high false-positive rates with manual analysis burdens that cause alert fatigue; in particular, existing implementations of the open-source SIEM Wazuh "lack direct integration with advanced AI capabilities" that could improve detection accuracy and responsiveness (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: SERC (Security Event Response Copilot): an LLM copilot embedded as a Copilot tab in the Wazuh SIEM dashboard, combining (1) security event data extraction via RAG and (2) LLM-based incident response guidance; a Pixtral-powered LLM extractor parses Wazuh JSON event logs (one-shot prompt), embeddings from BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 are stored in a Qdrant vector database (cosine similarity) across three collections — general incident response knowledge, NIST CSF 2.0, MITRE ATT&CK (with a service that periodically syncs MITRE updates); a prompt builder consolidates retrieved context and the LLM (GPT-4o or Pixtral 12B; temperature 0.1, top-k 50, top-p 0.9, max tokens 4096) generates tailored mitigation guidance, with a chat feature for analyst follow-up (human-in-the-loop) (Sec. 3.1-3.4, pp. 11-16; Sec. 4.1, pp. 16-17)
Methodology: Prototype implementation plus end-to-end attack-defense simulation: Atomic Red Team (Red Atomic Attack Emulator) executed six distinct attack types (categories listed: Account Compromise, Data Loss, Malware, Phishing, Ransomware) mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques (e.g., T1078, T1486, T1204.002) on a monitored endpoint with Wazuh agents; 12 attack scenarios evaluated; copilot recommendations compared against the SOCFortress Incident Response Plan ground truth using cosine similarity and BERTScore (precision, recall, F1), comparing two models (OpenAI GPT-4o vs. Pixtral 12B) (Sec. 4.2-4.3, pp. 17-19)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — no MTTD, MTTR, response-time, or latency measurements are reported; benefits to incident response speed are qualitative only (LLMs in SOC workflows can "mitigate analyst fatigue", reduce cognitive load, and accelerate decision-making) (Sec. 2.2, p. 4; Sec. 2.8, p. 10); evaluation instead measured response quality: cosine similarity — OpenAI peaked at 75.81% (scenario 8) and dropped to 46.61% (scenario 6), Pixtral up to 71.69% (scenario 9); BERTScore — Pixtral precision 84.5-87.0%, recall 85.6-87.5%, F1 85.4-87.2%; OpenAI recall 84.8-86.9%, F1 84.9-86.5% (Sec. 4.3, pp. 19-21)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Single-LLM copilot, not a multi-agent system; shows RAG as a flexible, scalable alternative to fine-tuning for SOC LLMs (real-time threat intelligence without retraining overhead) (Sec. 2.8, p. 10); model comparison found complementary strengths — Pixtral consistently stable (precision, recall, F1) but plateauing in some scenarios, OpenAI more adaptable but variable with dips in recall/F1 (Sec. 5, p. 21); orchestration overhead, cost, and autonomy level Not specified
Limitations / Future Work: Both models "demonstrate room for improvement" where alignment with ground truth proved challenging: Pixtral's performance plateaued in certain scenarios and OpenAI showed inconsistency balancing precision and recall; future work: fine-tuning both models with domain-specific datasets, scenario-specific training for phishing and ransomware, adversarial training and active learning with expert feedback, and extending the framework to integrate with SOAR systems for end-to-end automation of the incident response lifecycle (Sec. 5, p. 21)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is a concrete, reproducible instance of an LLM copilot for incident response embedded in an open-source SIEM (Wazuh), directly matching the thesis theme of Agentic AI copilots in incident response. Its RAG architecture (Qdrant + bge-large-en-v1.5 + three knowledge collections spanning NIST CSF 2.0, MITRE ATT&CK, and IR playbooks) offers a transferable design pattern for grounding copilot guidance in operational frameworks. The Atomic Red Team simulation with SOCFortress playbooks as ground truth, evaluated by cosine similarity and BERTScore, illustrates a quality-oriented evaluation protocol the thesis can adapt. Critically, it does not measure MTTD/MTTR, exposing the exact gap the thesis targets: quantifying time-to-detect and time-to-recover impacts of copilot assistance rather than only response-text quality.
Relevance Score: Medium — an LLM/RAG copilot for SOC incident response is directly adjacent to the thesis (single-agent LLM ops), but the study evaluates response quality (cosine similarity, BERTScore) and reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements.

Title: An LLM-Based Agentic Network Traffic Incident-Report Approach Towards Explainable-AI Network Defense
Authors: Chia-Hong Chou; Arjun Sudheer; Younghee Park
Year & Venue: 2026; Journal of Sensor and Actuator Networks (J. Sens. Actuator Netw., MDPI), vol. 15, article 32
Core Problem Addressed: Traditional ML/DL-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) for IoT networks achieve high classification accuracy but operate as black boxes, lacking interpretability and actionable incident-response capabilities, which undermines analyst trust and slows incident response; existing LLM-based security tools (ChatIDS, HuntGPT) explain alerts but do not produce evidence-grounded incident reports nor undergo rigorous faithfulness/groundedness evaluation (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Graph-based multi-agent framework with three sequential phases sharing a centralized pipeline state: (1) lightweight binary Random Forest pre-detection (top-10 MDI features, 6 MB, 99.49% accuracy) with early exit for benign traffic; (2) ensemble multi-class classification (MLP, Random Forest, XGBoost) aggregated by soft voting plus SHAP feature attribution for explainability; (3) a ReAct-based summary agent (LangGraph, Llama-3.1-8b-instant via Groq API, temperature 0.0, max 300 tokens) performing RAG with three tools — Tavily Web Search, ArXiv Search, and a Chroma DB internal knowledge base (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings) — to generate structured, evidence-grounded incident reports with mitigation recommendations; the authors advise treating reports as analyst-assistive drafts with human-in-the-loop review before dissemination (Sec. 3.1, pp. 6-8; Sec. 3.6, pp. 10-11; Sec. 4.5, pp. 28-29).
Methodology: Empirical prototype evaluation (controlled experiment) on the ACI IoT Network Dataset 2023: 1,170,570 network-flow records, 11 classes, 71 numerical features; 80/20 stratified train-test split with leakage-controlled preprocessing, 10-fold stratified cross-validation, and Optuna hyperparameter tuning; RAG output quality assessed via LLM-as-Judge (RAGAs framework, Llama-3.1-8b-instant judge) with custom faithfulness and groundedness metrics on 176 test samples (from 200 evaluation attempts, 24 errors excluded) (Sec. 3.2-3.3, p. 8; Sec. 3.7, pp. 11-14; Sec. 4.3, p. 23).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, and resolution-time metrics are not reported; as efficiency proxies, end-to-end inference from traffic ingestion to final report takes 2.9-11.6 s per malicious sample, pre-detection alone rendered 0.3 s latency, and the summary agent is framed as "reducing cognitive load and moving a step towards explainable and actionable network defense" (Sec. 4.4, p. 28; Sec. 4.5, p. 28; Sec. 3.6.3, p. 11).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Ensemble soft voting mitigates individual model weaknesses, improving the UDP Flood F1 score from 48% (MLP alone, 0.4828) to 95% (ensemble, 0.9515); the ensemble reached 99.7971% accuracy and 99.2284% macro F1; the RAG summary agent scored perfect groundedness (1.0000) and moderate faithfulness (0.6391, std 0.14) across 176 samples; agent overhead: average 5247 tokens per malicious sample (4689 prompt + 557 completion), ~560 tokens/s throughput, LLM cost $0.05/1M input and $0.08/1M output tokens, with the 2.9-11.6 s latency driven primarily by external tool calls (Sec. 4.2, pp. 16-22; Sec. 4.3, p. 23; Sec. 4.4, p. 28; Sec. 3.6, p. 10; Sec. 4.6, p. 29).
Limitations / Future Work: End-to-end latency of 2.9-11.6 s may not meet sub-second production IDS requirements (future: response caching, model distillation, asynchronous tool calls); SHAP and RAG contributions not formally ablated; SHAP unsupported for the MLP model (future: Integrated Gradients) and MLP remains weak on UDP Flood (F1: 0.4828); evaluation limited to the 11 known attack classes of a single dataset — zero-day/out-of-distribution detection not assessed (future: leave-one-class-out design); reliance on external cloud APIs (Groq, Tavily) introduces privacy risks and network dependency (future: quantized, fine-tuned local LLMs on edge devices) (Sec. 4.6, pp. 29-30).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper instantiates the Agentic AI copilot pattern central to my thesis: a ReAct-based LLM agent that converts detections into evidence-grounded incident reports explicitly positioned as analyst-assistive drafts with human-in-the-loop review, supporting the copilot (not fully autonomous) framing. Its faithfulness/groundedness LLM-as-Judge evaluation provides a reusable blueprint for assessing the quality of copilot-generated incident reports, a dimension complementary to MTTD/MTTR. The reported pipeline latency (2.9-11.6 s) and token/cost figures offer concrete proxies for the detection-to-report interval in incident response. However, the absence of incident-management metrics (MTTD, MTTR, resolution time) marks precisely the measurement gap my research addresses.
Relevance Score: Medium — an agentic LLM incident-report copilot with rigorous RAG evaluation directly adjacent to the thesis topic, but it does not measure MTTD/MTTR or other incident-management time metrics.

Title: A decentralised self-healing approach for network topology maintenance
Authors: Arles Rodríguez; Jonatan Gómez; Ada Diaconescu
Year & Venue: 2021; Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (JAAMAS, Springer), vol. 35, article 6; accepted 27 October 2020, published online 27 November 2020
Core Problem Addressed: Recovering large-scale distributed systems (server farms, clouds, sensor networks) from node failures while preserving the original network topology, on which reconfiguration cost, distributed algorithms and traffic performance strongly depend; downtimes can generate "losses of thousands of dollars per minute" and human experts "may be unable to react fast enough for dealing with multiple failures within short periods", so fast automated self-healing is needed — unlike prior work that only preserves connectivity or diameter, not topology (Sec. 1, p. 2; Sec. 2, p. 4).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A decentralised multi-agent self-healing approach with two mechanisms: (1) runtime collection/dissemination of topology data, via either mobile agents (the authors' proposal, moving with the 'random with marks' algorithm, carrying topology dictionaries and being discarded once their redundancy counter reaches k) or Trickle (RFC6206 "polite gossip" baseline adapted to discrete rounds, Imin=1 round, Imax=2^16 rounds, k=3); and (2) local node recovery: nodes are static agents that detect neighbour failures by comparing heartbeat-based perception at round t with memorised local topology at t-1, and the alive neighbour with the minimum node id recreates and reconnects the failed node, sharing its local topology data with the replica; fully autonomous, with no LLM and no human-in-the-loop (Sec. 3.3, pp. 7-8; Sec. 4.3, p. 16; Sec. 4.4, pp. 17-18).
Methodology: Agent-based simulation study documented with the ODD protocol, run in a multi-threaded multi-agent simulator on a single machine (source code on GitHub); six topologies: Small-world, Community, Scale-free, Hub & Spoke and Forest Hub & Spoke (~100 nodes each) plus the SNAP as19981231 Internet-router network (512 nodes, 1273 edges); node failure probability pf in {0.5, 0.25, 0}; each experiment repeated 30 times over 100 rounds (or (start, stop, end) failure intervals of 25+25 rounds after data-collection reference points); metrics: memory (bytes), bandwidth overhead (bytes), number of messages received, and network similarity (%) to the original topology via a neighbour-matching graph similarity metric (Sec. 3, pp. 6-12; Sec. 5.1, pp. 18-20; Sec. 5.2, p. 20).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — no MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue or incident resolution time metrics are reported; recovery is measured as network similarity over simulation rounds: with full prior topology knowledge all six networks recovered 100% at pf=0.25, and AS, Community and Small-world also at pf=0.5 (failed runs out of 30 at pf=0.5: Scale-free 6, Forest Hub & Spoke 7, Hub & Spoke 8); with runtime data-collection, similarity drops during the 25-round failure period and "recovers to 100% (or almost 100%)" after failures stop — mobile agents with k=3 on the AS network reached a median similarity of 99.95%, corrected to 100% by raising k to 5 (Sec. 5.2, Table 5, p. 20; Sec. 5.4, pp. 22-24).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Mobile agents achieved self-healing equivalent to the Trickle baseline while incurring lower bandwidth overheads ("up to 100% difference for the 'AS' network"; max RPD 105.63% in Table 7), because agents carry only partial, neighbourhood-local topology data — shown to suffice for full recovery even when failures start before collection completes; trade-offs: Trickle disseminates the complete topology faster (13 vs 38 rounds on AS) and exchanges fewer messages (mobile agents up to 146.08% RPD more, Hub & Spoke, Table 8, mostly lightweight 'visited-status' pings), while mobile agents consume up to 38% more total memory during collection on AS but up to 20% less once agents are dropped (Sec. 5.4, p. 22; Sec. 5.5, pp. 24-29, Tables 7-10; Sec. 5.6, pp. 29-33).
Limitations / Future Work: Stated assumptions: the number of simultaneously failing interconnected nodes is limited so repair outruns failures; nodes fail independently (internal failures only — not valid for interdependent networks); any node can be recreated/reconnected; uniqueness of node recreation relies on synchronous rounds and a dedicated ping channel — parallel node executions may create duplicates (future work); marginal nodes (degree 1-2) are prone to being lost at high pf; future work: determine the minimum neighbourhood information needed for recovery, prune transmitted topology data to a specific number of hops, evaluate scaling to networks orders of magnitude larger, adopt more sophisticated leader election, and apply the approach to container networks (Sec. 3.2, p. 6; Sec. 3.4, pp. 8-9; Sec. 4.4, pp. 17-18; Sec. 5.6, pp. 29-33; Sec. 6, pp. 33-34).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper supplies a classical (pre-LLM) multi-agent blueprint for the autonomous-remediation half of my thesis: heartbeat-based neighbour monitoring maps conceptually onto detection (MTTD) and decentralised node recreation onto recovery (MTTR), and its motivation — cloud downtimes costing thousands of dollars per minute with humans too slow to react — mirrors my problem framing. Its key empirical insight, that local neighbourhood knowledge suffices for full recovery, and its quantified orchestration trade-offs (bandwidth vs memory vs message overheads across topologies) inform how I can argue and measure the cost side of multi-agent incident-response designs. However, it is a simulation on abstract network topologies with no LLM copilot, no human-in-the-loop and no incident-management metrics, so it serves as background evidence on multi-agent self-healing rather than direct support for MTTD/MTTR reduction.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent work: a fully autonomous multi-agent self-healing approach for failure detection and recovery in distributed networks (cloud/data-centre motivation), but with no LLM/agentic copilot and no MTTD/MTTR measurement.
